title: Skillfully Discerning the Marks of All Dharmas
author: Zhanran
excerpt: Question: Please explain: "Skillfully discerning the marks of all dharmas, while remaining unmoving in the ultimate truth." (Vimalakirti Sutra)

inline.s: Question: Please explain:
"Skillfully discerning the marks of all dharmas, while remaining unmoving in the ultimate truth."
(Vimalakirti Sutra)

Answer: "The ultimate truth" is also called the ultimate-truth principle (paramārtha-satya), the supreme, unsurpassed, perfect, and ultimate truth. The true mark of all dharmas is the ultimate truth. The Buddha said:

"All dharmas are false and unreal; where they cease is what is called the real, what is called the true mark, what is called the dharma-realm, what is called ultimate wisdom, what is called the ultimate truth, what is called the ultimate emptiness."

Because we live in the dream of ignorance, this is a world of forms and marks. In order to survive and to practice, we must be able to discern well the marks of the various dharmas ("skillfully discerning the marks of all dharmas"). But we must not be turned by these illusory marks of dharmas, taking them to be true and so giving rise to feelings of love and hate and to intentions of grasping and rejecting. We must clearly know, and put into practice: all marks are illusory and false; do not grasp at marks, but remain thus, unmoving ("remaining unmoving in the ultimate truth"). We must know that living beings are originally Buddhas, and that it is only because of a single thought of ignorance that stirred in delusion, mistaking the marks of dharmas for real and being entangled by them, that they create karma, receive retribution, and pass through birth and death without end. Therefore, to be free of birth and death (birth and death in stages and birth and death of transformation), one must "remain unmoving in the ultimate truth" and cast off the entanglement of the marks of dharmas. The Shurangama Sutra says:

"All living beings, from beginningless time, continue in birth and death, all because they do not know the ever-abiding true mind, the pure, bright essence of their nature, and instead employ deluded thoughts; because these thoughts are not true, there is the turning of the wheel."

Translation: All living beings, from beginningless time, pass through birth and death in unbroken succession, all because they do not know the pure, bright essence of the true mind that ever abides in their nature, and instead employ deluded thoughts; because these deluded thoughts, which take illusion for reality, do not accord with the actual true mark of all dharmas, there is the turning of the wheel (there is birth and death in stages and birth and death of transformation).

[birth and death in stages] For beings in the three realms and six paths, on account of the ripening of good and evil karma, their lifespans all have their limits and their bodily forms all have their distinctions, and therefore their birth and death is called "birth and death in stages." To be free of birth and death in stages is to escape the cycle of rebirth and leave the three realms. [birth and death of transformation] The sages of the Three Vehicles have already cut off the delusions of views and thought and freed themselves from birth and death in stages. In the course of their cultivation of the Way, deluded thoughts gradually die away and realization gradually increases. Each stage of this migration between delusion and awakening differs from the next. The movement from an earlier stage to a later one is like a birth and death in itself, and hence it is called "birth and death of transformation." To be free of birth and death of transformation is to perfectly realize the fruit of Buddhahood.
Question: Please
explain:
"A single thought of unawareness
(fundamental ignorance)
gives rise to the three subtle marks; the perceived world as condition gives rise to the six coarse marks."
Answer:

This describes the process by which the self-nature, through fundamental ignorance, passes from awakening (the state of original nature) into delusion (the state of consciousness), giving rise to delusion, creating karma, and receiving retribution. The "three subtle and six coarse marks" are the nine deluded marks of arising and ceasing and transmigration that are manifested as the self-nature enters delusion: the mark of ignorance as karma, the mark of being able to see, the mark of perceived objects; and the mark of intellect, the mark of continuity, the mark of grasping, the mark of naming, the mark of producing karma, and the mark of suffering bound by karma. Of these, the first three arise from fundamental ignorance ("a single thought of unawareness gives rise to the three subtle marks"), and their marks are subtle, so they are called the "three subtle marks"; the latter six grow by taking the perceived world as their condition ("the perceived world as condition gives rise to the six coarse marks"), and their marks are coarse and evident, so they are called the "six coarse marks."

[fundamental ignorance] Fundamental ignorance is the very first stirring of thought. Because of this single thought arising and moving, the self-nature falls into long-night confusion, does not understand the truth, and gives rise to all delusions and afflictions.
The process of the "three subtle and six coarse marks" is as follows:
The three subtle marks":
1. The mark of ignorance as karma. The moving of the mind is karma, so "the stirring of the mind in unawareness (the first stirring of thought)" is called the mark of ignorance as karma.
2. The mark of being able to see. Relying on the preceding "mark of ignorance as karma," when the mind stirs, it is able to see.
3. The mark of perceived objects (the mark of what is seen). Relying on the preceding "mark of being able to see," because there is seeing, the perceived world manifests in delusion.
These three subtle marks take ignorance as their cause, and so it is also said: "Ignorance as the cause gives rise to the three subtle marks."
The six coarse marks":
1. The mark of intellect. Relying on the preceding "mark of perceived objects," the intellect arises in delusion and discriminates favorable and unfavorable, beautiful and ugly, love and hate.
2. The mark of continuity. Relying on the preceding "mark of intellect," through the discrimination of the perceived world, one thinks and calculates, and thoughts continue one after another.
3. The mark of grasping. Relying on the preceding "mark of continuity," the continuous thoughts deepen and give rise to self and mine, forming the mark of grasping.
4. The mark of naming. Relying on the preceding "mark of grasping," one names the various realms, things, and objects, forming concepts and language.
5. The mark of producing karma. Relying on the preceding "mark of naming," through thinking and calculating, one creates the various kinds of karma of body, speech, and mind.

6. The mark of suffering bound by karma. Relying on the preceding "mark of producing karma," one is bound by the karma of body, speech, and mind that one has created, and so experiences the bitter fruit of birth and death.
These six coarse marks grow by taking the perceived world as their condition, and so it is said: "The perceived world as condition gives rise to the six coarse marks."
Among the
nine deluded marks
, the first seven (
the mark of ignorance as karma
the mark of being able to see
the mark of perceived objects
the mark of intellect
the mark of continuity
the mark of grasping
the mark of naming
) are delusion
the eighth (
the mark of producing karma
) is karma
and the ninth (
the mark of suffering bound by karma
) is suffering
A sutra says:
"Through delusion karma is created; through karma suffering is received."
This is the process of passing from awakening into delusion.

Therefore, the process by which the self-nature passes from awakening into delusion, until it is bound by karma and suffers, is: the stirring of the mind in unawareness (the arising of thought) → the arising of the roots and consciousness, which are able to see → the manifestation of the perceived world → discrimination → deluded thinking (thinking and calculating, thoughts continuing one after another) → grasping (running after desires and thoughts) → creating karma → suffering bound by karma.

And returning to the origin is simply reversing the above process, passing from delusion into awakening: suffering bound by karma → not creating karma → not grasping (not running after desires and thoughts) → not deluded thinking → not discriminating → the extinction of the perceived world → turning consciousness into wisdom, so that the roots and consciousness cease → the cessation of the subtle stream.

[turning consciousness into wisdom] Turning the eight consciousnesses into the four wisdoms: turning the defiled first five consciousnesses (eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness) into the undefiled wisdom of accomplishing deeds; turning the defiled sixth consciousness (mind-consciousness) into the undefiled wisdom of wondrous observation; turning the defiled seventh consciousness (manas) into the undefiled wisdom of equality; turning the defiled eighth consciousness (alaya) into the undefiled great perfect mirror wisdom. [defilement] another name for affliction, containing the two meanings of leaking and falling. The afflictions of greed, anger, and so on leak and stream forth day and night from the six sense faculties without cease, and so are called "leaks"; and because afflictions can make a person fall into the three evil realms, they are also called "leaks." All dharmas that possess affliction are called "defiled dharmas," and dharmas without affliction are called "undefiled dharmas." [the four wisdoms] the wisdom of accomplishing deeds, the wisdom of wondrous observation, the wisdom of equality, and the great perfect mirror wisdom. The "wisdom of accomplishing deeds" is the wisdom that accomplishes all deeds that universally benefit living beings; the "wisdom of wondrous observation" is the wisdom that observes all dharmas and the capacities of all living beings, giving medicine according to the illness and turning the ordinary into the sage; the "wisdom of equality" is the wisdom that penetrates the principle of selflessness and equality, and toward all living beings arouses great compassion that is without conditions; the "great perfect mirror wisdom" is the wisdom that clearly sees all phenomena and principles without exception — this wisdom is pure, perfect, and bright, seeing within and without thoroughly, like a great perfect mirror that clearly reflects all things.
